title: Template-free synthesis of colloidal quantum dot assemblies with molecule-like architectures

paper_content.abstract: Designing colloidal assemblies with molecule-like architectures comprising more than two electronically coupled quantum dots has often required technologically complex, expensive, and top-down nanofabrication. Here we demonstrate a one-pot chemical synthesis of dimeric, trimeric, and tetrameric assemblies of coupled molecule-like quantum dots (CMQDs), using ZnSe@ZnS quantum dots as model. We show that the “valence” of these “artificial atoms” can be readily tuned by the amount of a suitable ligand in the reaction mixture, and that high-temperature fusion yields highly ordered oriented attachment and strong electron coupling between bound QDs. The shapes of the fused assemblies echo the canonical sp-, sp²-, and sp³-hybridization motifs and can be interpreted as appropriately shaped confining potential wells for electrons and holes. This work establishes an experimentally accessible entry point to related “artificial molecules” with controllable chemical composition, geometry, and electronic structure. The enhanced or emergent properties of such nanomaterials are anticipated to advance applications in optoelectronics, sensing, and quantum photonic technologies.
paper_content.introduction:
All modern technology is unthinkable without scientists’ ability to arrange atoms into specific molecules/matter with precise control over chemical composition, geometry, and as a result, electronic structure. That same “control mindset” is now being transferred to nanoscale building blocks. For example, semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are widely viewed as artificial atoms1-4 because quantum confinement gives them discrete, atom-like electronic structure, tunable by size, composition, and surface chemistry. Such paradigm has already inspired several applications of QDs as lasers,5single-photon sources,6 source of entangled photon pairs.7 However, fully exploiting the potential of artificial atoms requires learning how to synthesize quantum dot “molecules” with controlled stoichiometry, programmed geometry, and engineered electronic coupling between bound QDs. The latter generates emergent “molecular” electronic states and functions beyond those of isolated artificial atoms,8-13 thus enabling the design of new materials and devices for optoelectronics, quantum photonics, nanoscale energy/charge transport technologies and many other fields.

Molecule-like quantum dot assemblies can be differentiated by the nature of the inter-QD linkage. We define self-assembled quantum dot molecules as finite, stoichiometrically and geometrically distinct QD aggregates whose integrity is governed primarily by the interactions of function al groups on their periphery. To date, several successful strategies have been developed for the programmed synthesis of assembled quantum dot molecules, relying on DNA-encoded recognition motifs,14-16 electrostatic comple mentarity of charged polymer brushes,17 or templated multi-step procedure that allows to bind two QD particles with short covalent links (≈1 nm).18 All such linkages can provide exquisite control over the directionality, connectivity, and symmetry of assembled quantum dot molecules, but they inevitably impede inter-dot electronic communication.19

In contrast, in coupled colloidal molecule-like quantum dots (CMQDs),20 adjacent QD “atoms” form direct core–core junctions, yielding a rigid, chemically robust backbone of fused QDs and enabling direct electronic and energy coupling and, potentially, dopant exchange across the entire CMQDs. Yet, the reliable synthesis of such coupled dots21 remains considerably less straightforward than the assembly of assembled quantum dot molecules. Direct nanofabrication via molecular beam epitaxy,22, 23 though precise and compatible with convenient fabrication of CMQDs-based devices, is technologically complex, expensive, and difficult to scale. Much more practical is a templated approach24 in which assembled quantum dot molecules with short covalent linkages serve as intermediates for subsequent fusion into CMQDs. While reliable, this workflow is experimentally involved and was only extended to dimeric assembled quantum dot assembles.

In this work, we present a template-free, one-pot methodology for the synthesis of CMQDs via controlled fusion of two, three, or four QDs. ZnSe@ZnS quantum dots (Figure 1a) and their Cu- or Mn-doped variants were used to demonstrate our approach and to test the basic properties of the synthesized CMQDs. The exact outcome of the synthesis depends on the optimized amount of added oleylamine (OLAm). Atomic-resolution imaging corroborates face-to-face oriented attachment (OA) of the fused nanoparticles and allows us to postulate a dynamic combinatorial transformation of closely packed dimeric, triangular, and tetrahedral assembled quantum dot intermediates, as the connectivity (“valency”) of each individual QD increases with increasing OAm quantity. The fused CMQDs backbones can be viewed as continuous confining potential wells for electrons and holes, with overall geometries reminiscent of the canonical linear, trigonal, and tetrahedral motifs associated with sp, sp², and sp³ hybridization, respectively. In addition to advanced optical characterization, these quantum dot assemblies were evaluated as X-ray scintillators.
paper_content.results:
Synthesis of colloidal molecule-like assemblies
The fabrication of CMQDs was derived from colloidal ZnSe/ZnS core/shell QDs25, 26 via modulation of the Ostwald ripening (OR), oriented attachment (OA), and multistep oriented attachment (MOA) process (Figure 1a and Supplementary Fig.1). Briefly, oleate and OLAm, as typical hard bases, exhibit strong coordination with zinc ions (borderline Lewis acids), resulting in effective passivation of the ZnSe/ZnS surface and the formation of monodisperse QDs.27 Meanwhile, OLAm acts as an amine-based anchor, whereas oleic acid (OLA) predominantly appears as a monodentate carboxylate that links the long-chain alkyl tail to the QD surface, with the carboxylate remaining more stable than the amine even in the monodentate form.28 Thus, when the solvent is exchanged from OLA/OLAm to pure OLAm, the passivation effect becomes insufficient, resulting in enhanced oriented attachment and the formation of ZnSe/ZnS dimers.29 When excess pure OLAm is introduced into the system, the viscosity of the reaction medium increases significantly,28 reducing the diffusion rate of the building blocks and promoting a MOA process, accompanied by Ostwald ripening and the formation of timer and tetramer ZnSe/ZnS molecules (Supplementary Figs. 2-5). Therefore, as the OLA concentration decreases and the OLAm amount increases, the self-organized, self-driven structure formed via multistep oriented attachment leads to the predominant formation of tetramer ZnSe/ZnS QDs.

Characterization and binding relationship analysis
We selected colloidal monomer ZnSe/ZnS QDs as the fundamental building blocks. The dimer, trimer, and tetramer colloidal molecules were fabricated in analogy with the sp, sp², and sp³ hybrid atomic orbitals, respectively (Figure 1b). The morphology of the ZnSe/ZnS CMQDs is depicted in Figure 1c-n and Supplementary Fig. 6. The monomer ZnSe/ZnS QDs were synthesized using the hot-injection method, with slight modifications based on refs.30-34 (see Methods). As depicted in Figure 1c-e, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), and high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF-STEM) imaging confirmed the fabrication of monomer QDs with low dispersity in size of 8.4 ± 1.9 nm (Supplementary Fig. 6). Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern and X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) measurements indicate the zinc blende (ZB) structure of the ZnSe/ZnS QD building blocks (Supplementary Fig. 6). The dimer (Figure 1f-h), timer (Figure 1i-k), and tetramer (Figure 1l-n) structures were further characterized. HAADF-STEM images show that the fabricated monomer, dimer, trimer, and tetramer colloidal molecules closely resemble the hybridization atomic orbital model, including similarities in bond angles. Consequently, by decreasing the amount of OLA and increasing the amount of OLAm, the OR process is suppressed, allowing the OA and multistep OA processes to dominate, thereby facilitating the synthesis of ZnSe/ZnS CMQDs.

The fine structure of the ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs was further characterized using HAADF-STEM imaging and the corresponding 3D reconstructed structure. As shown in Figure 2a, the low index atomic planes (111), (020), and (202) are clearly visible, which facilitates identification of the boundary faces of the monomer crystal model (Figure 2b). Fast Fourier transform (FFT) analysis and the FFT-filtered reconstructed atomic structure (Supplementary Fig. 7) confirmed the zinc blende (ZB) ZnSe@ZnS structure along the [101] zone axis (ZA). To further validate the constructed monomer crystal model, structural analysis along the [01̅0] ZA was depicted in Supplementary Fig. 8. This analysis demonstrates the accurate reconstruction of cubic motifs35, which will serve as the model structure for subsequent oriented attachment relationship analysis.

The structure of the coupled colloidal ZnSe@ZnS dimer molecules (Figure 2c) was confirmed through HAADF-STEM imaging, which revealed a continuous atomic lattice formed between the two adjoined monomer QDs. This observation confirms the dimer structure through mutual modulation of the OA processes. A hetero-plane oriented attachment was observed, characterized by the connection of heteronymous faces: (022) ||(211) , matched well with the 3D ZnSe@ZnS dimer QD model (Figure 2d) derived from the STEM analysis. In this hetero-plane attachment scenario, both ZnSe@ZnS monomers in the conjunctive pair were further analyzed using separated FFT pattern analysis, revealing the fusion axes along [011] ZA and [213] ZA , respectively(Supplementary Fig. 9). Additionally, both homonymous (Supplementary Fig. 10) and heteronymous (misorientation) plane attachment relationships are observed in our system.

The sp2-analog trimer structure was characterized using HAADF-STEM (Figure 2e). It is clearly observed that the ternary structure is formed by connecting of a third monomer to a homonymous dimer QD. Both parts A and A of the trimer structure are aligned along the same [1̅21] zone axis, resulting in the formation of a homonymous plane attachment: (202) ||(202) (Figure 2f, and Supplementary Fig. 11). Notably, the size of the third monomer part (A ) in the ternary QDs is significantly smaller than that of the other two parts, attributed to the highly active vestigial monomer based on the incomplete inhibition of the Ostwald ripening effect. This phenomenon is also observed in the quaternary QD structures (Figure 2g, h, and Supplementary Fig. 12). It is evident that parts A toA exhibit similar geometric symmetry with a twisting or twirling effect along the [1̅21] ZA. Additionally, a fourth smaller monomer connects to the trimer structure along the [01̅1] ZA. This connection helps alleviate surface strain when forming trimer or tetramer colloidal ZnSe@ZnS assemblies with constrained attachment.

Significant surface defects are typically observed during the formation of trimer and tetramer CMQDs due to the combined modulation of the OR and OA processes. These defects36, 37 include stacking faults, edge dislocations, twin boundaries, and grain boundaries (details in Supplementary Fig. 13, 14), particularly in the tetramer structure. Additionally, multi-branched multimer QDs are observed during tetramer formation (Supplementary Fig. 15). Furthermore, energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) element mapping confirmed the core-shell architecture of the colloidal ZnSe@ZnS assemblies (Figure 2i-l), which indicating a continuous distribution of zinc in both the core and shell locations, while sulfur and selenium are distinctly located, signifying the shell and core positions, respectively. Thus, by precisely controlling the effects of the ligands via OR, and OA, and tuning them together, we synthesized monomer, dimer, trimer, and tetramer ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs.

Photophysical properties
The optical signatures of the assemblies were further explored as shown in Figure 3a,b. The coupled quantum dot assemblies exhibit significant red shifts in band-edge absorption and photoluminescence (PL) compared to the ZnSe@ZnS monomer. Additionally, according to the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) pattern, the formation of tetramer ZnSe@ZnS assemblies resulted in an almost pure blue emission (Figure 3c). This emission approaches the limits of ZnSe-based QDs, which still presents a challenge, requiring further investigation. Notably, a red shift of 71.3 meV was observed for the type-I ZnSe@ZnS tetramer compared to the monomer QDs. In contrast, our previous quasi-type II CdSe@CdS coupled dimer structure exhibited only a 26 meV red shift.38 Meanwhile, ensemble PL lifetime measurements revealed quenching of the lifetime (Figure 3d). The calculation results show that the electron and hole ground states in the monomer, dimer, trimer, and tetramer are confined to the core (Figure 3e, Supplementary Note 1, and Supplementary Table 1). The first excited state of the electron is confined to both the core and the shell. The red shift of the dimer, trimer, and tetramer relative to the monomer can be attributed to the coupling of the wave functions in the different quantum dots, analogous to the symmetry and antisymmetric of wave functions in conventional molecules (Figure 3f, g). We hypothesize that the formation of larger molecules and increased volume during the OA/OR combined process may lead to coupling with electron dislocation. This could result in observed red shifts in both absorption and PL, accompanied by lifetime quenching, reflecting the coupling among quantum dot assemblies and analogous to chemical bond-type hybridization seen in carbon-based systems.

To further validate our hypothesis, we conducted femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (fs-TAS) measurements, as depicted in Figure 3h-o. A prominent negative peak (ΔA<0) is observed around 430 nm and is attributed to ground-state bleaching (GSB). This reflects the depopulation of photo-generated electrons in the excitons of the ZnSe@ZnS QDs. When irradiated with a 365 nm pump laser, excitons are immediately generated and dissociated into free holes and electrons in the ZnSe@ZnS QDs. High-energy electrons then recombine with holes within 2.0 ps. Notably, ground state bleaching rapidly decays with the formation of colloidal ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs, indicating a fast exciton recombination rate. This rapid recombination may be due to energy transfer or surface defect trapping processes (Supplementary Fig. 16). Furthermore, a shift in GSB to longer wavelengths occurs as the decay time increases from 2.0 ps to 2.0 ns. This shift is likely due to the QDs’ significant volume increase, which results in enhanced electron dislocation and/or spatial separation rates 39-43and facilitates faster charge separation.

Single-particle photoluminescence spectroscopy
We investigate the PL properties of ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs at the single-particle level using single-particle PL spectroscopy. 44 As shown in Figure 4a-c, the single monomer, dimer and trimer CMQDs all exhibit stable PL intensity trajectories. The corresponding PL intensity histograms demonstrate that they all exhibit a significant proportion of bright states. This indicates that these monomers, dimers and trimers were prepared to a high standard. Due to the QDs' surfaces being passivated, the monomer exhibits a standard Auger blinking trajectory, as revealed by the nonlinear fluorescence lifetime-intensity distribution (FLID) 45 map shown in Supplementary Fig. 17. The corresponding PL decay curves which exhibit a multiexponential characteristic due to the influence of multi-excitons, ionized states, and surface non-radiative recombination, are shown in Figure 4d-f. A multi-exponential function fit yielded weighted average lifetimes of 19.7, 17.5, and 15.9 ns for the monomer, dimer and trimer assemblies, respectively. This gradual decrease in lifetime is attributed to an increase in multiple excitons and surface non-radiative recombination in the dimer and trimer assemblies. Single exciton lifetimes were obtained by fitting the PL decay curves extracted from the bright state of the PL intensity trajectories (Supplementary Fig. 18a-c), and the statistical results are summarized in Supplementary Fig 18d. The average single-exciton lifetimes in monomers, dimers and trimers are 25.3, 26.4, and 26.9 ns, respectively. This indicates that forming multimeric structures does not significantly alter the radiative recombination properties of single excitons.

The second-order photon correlation, (g(2)(τ)), curves are shown in Figure 4g-i and reveal the statistics of photons from single ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs. Under low excitation, the biexciton QY was approximately equal to g(2)(0).46 The g(2)(0) statistics for monomers, dimers, and trimers are in Figure 4j-l, with values clustering around 0.37, 0.58, and 0.65, respectively. Specifically, monomers show a narrow distribution due to high purity; dimers are broader, reflecting slightly lower purity, and trimers are also broad, consistent with STREM yields (Supplementary Table 2). Dimers and trimers have higher g(2)(0) than monomers due to segregated biexcitons (SBX), which are long-lived, spatially separated biexcitons with reduced Auger quenching.47 Biexciton PL decay was further analyzed from the first photon in two-photon events.48 Dimer decays fall into two types: (i) rapid decay fitted by a single exponential, from strongly coupled dimers where both excitons reside in one core (localized biexciton, LBX; Figure 4m and left panel of Figure 4o), and (ii) a double-exponential decay with a fast LBX and slow SBX component (Figure 4n). In strongly coupled dimers, SBX converts quickly to LBX; in weakly coupled dimers, SBX and LBX emissions coexist due to slower SBX to LBX conversion.47 Supplementary Fig. 19 shows SBX lifetimes are broadly distributed due to coupling heterogeneity. Supplementary Fig. 20 reports LBX lifetimes of 1.7 ns (monomer), 2.3 ns (dimer), and 2.7 ns (trimer), with longer LBX lifetimes in dimers/trimers arising from enhanced exciton delocalization that suppresses Auger recombination.

Supplementary Fig. 21 shows the power-dependent PL decay for single monomer, dimer, and trimer assemblies.49 As laser power increases, the decay becomes faster, indicating a larger fraction of biexcitons at higher excitation. Power-dependent decay measurements thus quantify both biexciton lifetimes and Auger recombination, by subtracting high- and low-power decays. The extracted biexciton lifetimes are 2.03 ns (monomer), 2.24 ns (dimer), and 2.33 ns (trimer) (Supplementary Fig. 21d-f), consistent with the LBX lifetimes from the first-photon analysis in Supplementary Fig. 20. It should be noted that the biexciton lifetime can reach up to 2 ns, likely due to an alloyed ZnSe/ZnS shell that reduces Auger recombination, in line with recent report50. Additionally, an excess carrier may occupy the second emission center in the dimer, forming a potential trion (Supplementary Fig. 22). Meanwhile, the dimer and trimer assemblies exhibit more blinking in their PL trajectories due to band-edge carrier (BC) blinking, which is induced by surface defects formed during synthesis.51 Auger and BC blinking are caused by non-radiative Auger recombination and non-radiative BC recombination, respectively (Figure 4p). Additionally, due to the weak PL features, it was difficult to investigate the PL properties of individual tetramer assemblies at the single-particle level; only fast PL decay lifetimes could be obtained (Supplementary Fig. 23).

X-ray scintillator application
To further explore the boundaries of ZnSe@ZnS QD-based CMQDs structures, we synthesized doped ZnSe@ZnS QDs. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 24, the effects of different Mn2+ doping concentrations were investigated. An optimal Mn doping concentration of around 8% was found to achieve the highest PL quantum yield (QY) (detailed in Supplementary Fig. 25). Additionally, Cu²⁺-doped ZnSe:Cu@ZnS was fabricated using a similar strategy (Supplementary Figs. 26, 27). The ZnSe:Mn@ZnS was then used as a building block to synthesize colloidal molecule-like structures.

As illustrated in Figure 5a-d and Supplementary Fig. 28, STEM imaging confirms the formation of monomer, dimer, trimer, and tetramer ZnSe:Mn@ZnS QDs. The XRD pattern depicted in Figure 5e indicates that the coupled assemblies maintain the typical ZB structure even after Mn²⁺ doping. Similar red shifts are observed in the absorption and emission spectra of the ZnSe:Mn@ZnS-based system (Figure 5f, g). Due to surface strain, the PL feature of the tetramer structure is diminished. Meanwhile, the coupled assemblies based on ZnSe:Mn@ZnS exhibit rapid quenching of the PL lifetime (Figure 5h). Thus, the synthesis of ZnSe:Mn@ZnS assemblies demonstrates their versatility and potential application in Cd or Pd-based molecular structures.

Inspired by their fast charge separation rate and potential to avoid re-absorption, we investigated their application in X-ray scintillation. ZnSe is known as a scintillator candidate, particularly in ZnSe:Ag@ZnS materials52. Currently, zinc-based structures are primarily used for α particle detection. However, their use in X-ray imaging or detection is limited due to issues such as in stability, susceptibility to deliquescence, and strong reabsorption effects. We propose that our surface-engineered strategy for colloidal assemblies, which facilitates a fast charge separation rate, will provide promising candidates for improved performance and address these challenges.

The X-ray radio-luminescence spectrum shown in Supplementary Fig. 29 exhibits a consistent trend with the UV-induced luminescence spectrum. This indicates that there is a similar efficient energy transfer process under both X-ray and UV excitation. To demonstrate the potential application of ZnSe:Mn@ZnS in X-ray scintillation, we evaluated the X-ray imaging properties of scintillation films using an X-ray imaging system (Supplementary Fig. 30). X-ray imaging of the ZnSe:Mn@ZnS dimer, compared with monomer samples, reveals that the designed structure can distinguish different spring and SUDA markers clearly (Figure 5i), whereas images produced by ZnSe@ZnS appear blurry and dark. Therefore, the ZnSe:Mn@ZnS dimer system inhibits self-absorption due to its large Stokes shift and exhibits X-ray scintillator imaging performance due to its high energy transfer efficiency. Figure 5j proposes a plausible mechanism for the radioluminescence of ZnSe:Mn@ZnS nanocrystals. During the initial conversion phase, X-ray photons primarily interact with the lattice atoms of the ZnSe:Mn@ZnS nanocrystals, generating a significant number of high-energy electrons and holes. Subsequently, secondary electrons and low-kinetic charge carriers are produced. These charge carriers dissipate thermally through interactions with phonons, resulting in the transport of secondary electrons and holes into the conduction and valence bands52, respectively. However, due to the presence of Mn²⁺, the conduction band electrons do not directly recombine with the holes. Instead, they recombine with Mn²⁺, shifting the luminescence center to Mn²⁺. This behavior highlights the potential application of colloidal artificial ZnSe:Mn@ZnS CMQDs.

In summary, we have demonstrated template-free, one-pot, solution-based route to complex CMQDs. The discovery that the “valence” of artificial atoms can be easily modulated by varying the concentration of suitable ligands enables the programmed formation and subsequent fusion of few-dot assemblies into rigid, electronically coupled backbones of the desired CMQDs. The synthesized dimeric, trimeric, and tetrameric ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs can be regarded as confining potential wells shaped analogously to canonical sp, sp², and sp³ hybridization, respectively. In future work, we will elucidate the molecular mechanism by which ligands with low molecular weight (in the present study, oleylamine and oleic acid) modulate the valence of ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs and adapt this methodology to the synthesis of CMQDs from chemically distinct artificial atoms. Overall, our findings provide an experimentally accessible entry point toward solution-based synthesis of complex-shaped CMQDs, opening opportunities for emergent properties and applications in optoelectronics, sensing, and quantum technologies.
paper_content.methods:
Materials. Oleylamine (OLAm, 70%), 1-octadecene (ODE, 90%), oleic acid (OLA, 90%), zinc acetate (ZnAc , 2 99.99%), manganese acetate (MnAc , 99%) and 1-octanehiol (98%) were purchased from Thermo Scientific. Selenium powder (Se, 99.99%) was purchased from Tokyo Chemical Industry. Tri-n-octylphosphine (TOP 97%) and poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA, (C H O ) , M 35000 g mol-1) were purchased from Innochem. Toluene (C H , 5 8 2 n w 7 8 AR) and cyclohexane (C H , AR) were purchased from Beijing chemical works. All the reagents were used as 6 12 received without further purification

Synthesis of Zn(OLA) precursors. Zinc acetate dihydrate (1834.8 mg), oleic acid (OLA, 16 mL), and octadecene (ODE, 24 mL) were added to a 100 mL flask at room temperature under a nitrogen atmosphere. The mixture was then heated to 120 °C and degassed three times to remove residual water and oxygen. After degassing, nitrogen was reintroduced, and the mixture was maintained at 120 °C for 30 min, during which it gradually transformed from an initial white turbidity to a clear yellow solution. Once the reaction was complete, the mixture was cooled to 80 °C, and zinc oleate (Zn(OLA)₂) was obtained and transferred for further use. The Zn(OLA)₂ solution should be stored at 4 °C for subsequent experiments.

Synthesis of Mn(OLA) precursors. Manganese (II) acetate (MnAc₂, 865.2 mg), oleic acid (OLA, 9 mL), and 1-octadecene (11 mL) were added to a 100 mL flask at room temperature under a nitrogen atmosphere. The mixture was then heated to 120 °C and degassed three times to remove residual water and oxygen. After degassing, nitrogen was reintroduced, and the mixture was maintained at 120 °C for 30 min, during which it gradually transformed from an initial white turbidity to a clear yellow solution. Once the reaction was complete, the mixture was cooled to 80 °C, and manganese oleate (Mn(OLA)₂) was obtained and transferred for further use. The Mn(OLA)₂ solution should be stored at 4 °C for subsequent experiments.

Synthesis of ZnSe@ZnS QDs. A mixture of 1 mL OLAm, 1 mL oleic acid, 8 mL octadecene, and 1.6 mL Zn(OLA)₂ was added to a 50 mL four-neck flask and stirred at 800 rpm. After purging three times with nitrogen, it was heated to 120 °C for 30 min, then raised to 300°C under nitrogen53. A 1 mL Se stock solution was rapidly injected at 300 °C; after 5 min, the heater was removed to cool. When it reached 220 °C, 0.2 mL TOP was added, then cooled to 200 °C. When the temperature was raised back at 260 °C, two solutions were injected via pump over 2 h: 5 mL of 0.1 M Zn precursor and 5 mL of 0.13 M 1-octanethiol in ODE. The mixture was held at 295 °C for 30 min54, 55. The reaction was cooled to 180 °C, then 2 mL toluene was added. After cooling to room temperature, the product was centrifuged with ethanol, washed twice, and finally dissolved in 5 mL cyclohexane for storage.

Synthesis of ZnSe@ZnS dimers, trimers, and tetramers QDs. The procedure follows the same steps as the monomer synthesis, with variations only in the initial solvent composition56-58. For dimers, use 1 mL OLAm and 9 mL ODE; for trimers, 2 mL OLAm and 8 mL ODE; and for tetramers, 7 mL OLAm and 3 mL ODE. All other steps and reagent quantities remain consistent with the monomer protocol.

Synthesis of ZnSe:Mn@ZnS QDs. A mixture of 1 mL OLAm, 1 mL OLA, 8 mL ODE, 160 μL of 0.25 M manganese precursor, and 1.44 mL of 0.25 M zinc precursor was added to a 50 mL four-neck flask. The mixture was stirred at 800 rpm, then purged and degassed three times with nitrogen at room temperature. It was gradually heated to 120 °C and maintained for 30 min under nitrogen flow. The system was then switched to a nitrogen atmosphere and heated to 300 °C. Then, 1 mL selenium solution was rapidly injected and the reaction was maintained at 300 °C for 5 min before the heater was removed to cool the mixture. At 220 °C, 0.2 mL of TOP was injected, and the mixture was cooled to 200 °C59. When temperature was then increased to 240 °C, 0.6 mL of 0.25 M zinc precursor was slowly injected, followed by a 30-min reaction at 280 °C. The temperature was then raised to 295 °C. During heating, two solutions were pumped over 2 h: solution A, 0.1 M zinc precursor (5 mL with injection rate 2.5 mL h-1), and solution B, 0.13 M octanethiol in ODE (5 mL with injection rate 2.5 mL h-1). The mixture was maintained at 295 °C for 30 min, then cooled to 180 °C. 2 mL of toluene were added, and the solution was cooled to room temperature. The mixture was transferred to a centrifuge tube, mixed with ≈ 20 mL of anhydrous ethanol, and centrifuged at 11,000 × g for 10 min. The pellet was dissolved in 5 mL of cyclohexane, washed twice with ethanol, and the supernatant was collected for storage.

Synthesis of ZnSe:Mn@ZnS dimers, trimers, and tetramers QDs. The procedure follows the same steps as the monomer synthesis, differing only in the initial solvent composition: dimers use 2 mL OLAm and 8 mL ODE; trimers use 3.5 mL OLAm and 6.5 mL ODE; and tetramers use 7 mL OLAm and 3 mL ODE. All other steps and reagent quantities are identical to the monomer protocol reported in refs.60, 61.

Fabrication of QDs-PMMA. Briefly, 1.2 g of PMMA was dissolved in 8 mL of toluene and stirred at 50 °C for 1 h. Subsequently, the prepared QDs were added to the PMMA precursor and stirred at room temperature for an additional hour. The resulting mixture (QDs and PMMA colloid) was then poured onto a pre-fabricated template and dried either through annealing or air drying to produce the QDs@PMMA films.

Single-particle optical measurement. The optical measurement system based on a laser confocal microscopy platform was employed to investigate the single-photon properties of individual particles. Before the experiment, a quantum dot solution was applied to an acetone-cleaned slide after oscillation and spinning. During the measurement, a supercontinuum laser (NKT Photonics, EXW-12) with a central wavelength of 402 nm, a pulse width of 4 nm, and a repetition rate of 5 MHz served as the excitation source. The laser beam was reflected by a dichroic mirror and focused onto the sample through an oil immersion objective (OLYMPUS, 100×, 1.3 NA) to form a diffraction-limited spot. The emitted fluorescence from the quantum dots was collected by the same objective and directed to two single-photon detectors (Excelitas, SPCM-AQRH-16-FC) configured for Hanbury-Brown-Twiss measurements. Photon arrival times were recorded using a time-resolved, time-dependent single-photon counting (TTTR-TCSPC) data acquisition card (SImINICS, FT1040). The fluorescence decay curves, lifetimes, and second-order correlation functions were extracted from the data using MATLAB analysis software.

Characterization. The UV-vis-NIR absorption spectrum was measured using a Lambda 35 spectrophotometer. Photoluminescence and radioluminescence spectra were recorded with a QE Pro fluorescence spectrophotometer (Ocean Insight), equipped with a miniature X-ray source (AMPEK, mini-X2). X-ray-induced luminescence images were captured using a digital camera (Work Power WP-GS1200). Time-resolved photoluminescence measurements were conducted with a FL3-TCSPC system (HORIBA JOBIN YVON). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) analyses were performed with a Talos F200S G2 microscope operated at 200 kV. High-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) imaging and elemental mapping were carried out using a Themis Z aberration-corrected STEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 300 kV, equipped with a high angular annular dark field (HAADF) detector for STEM imaging and a Super-X energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) detector for elemental analysis. X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) measurements were performed with a D8 Advance diffractometer.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors present a nice study of controllably assemble collodial Zn-based nanoparticles to (monomers,) dimers, trimers and tetramers. The final strucutres resemble molecular bonding in terms of (s,) sp, sp2, and sp3 bonding. They discuss the corresponding mechanisms (beyond basic characterization) by crystallographic considerations and facetting. Further they explore the resulting optical properties and mechanisms in detail (time-resolved etc.)
I think this study can be published in Nature Communications since it is also well written.
I have only once request: The authors should add statistics of how many particles end up in the desired configuration as dimers, trimers and tetramers; how reliable is they synthesis ... does every approach lead to the desired outcome of does the outcome determine purpose; how many synthesis lead to the same predefined result?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript by Fan et al. presents a variation of colloidal molecules from ZnSe@ZnS nanocrystals. By slight modification of the synthesis that rebalances oriented attachment and Ostwald ripening, monomers, dimers, trimers and oligomers are created and studied with various TEM and optical spectroscopy methods. Furthermore, colloidal molecules from Mn-doped nanocrystals are investigated for their use as scintillator material. While the TEM studies appear clear and sound, I have several concerns on the spectroscopy results and interpretations, see further below.
Despite the claims in the abstract and introduction, the assembly of nanocrystals into colloidal molecules is far from novel, as it has been established for many nanocrystal material systems over the past decades, e.g. extensive works by the Manna group, or particularly related, CdSe dimers by the Banin group https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.accounts.0c00691 . Given the little actual change in the optical properties that the evolution from monomer over dimer and trimer to tetramer brings about (Figs. 3,4), it is questionable what benefits and tuning capabilities the presented colloidal molecules offer. Moreover, it is well known that doping nanocrystals enhances their properties for the use in scintillators through energy transfer and reduced reabsorption (see e.g. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.opelre.2019.01.001 ), but the current manuscript does not present significant advantages from using colloidal molecules for this application.
In conclusion, I fail to recognize “significant impact on quantum optoelectronics, sensing and high-energy particle detection” as the authors claim or a significant advance for the field that I would expect from a publication in Nature Communications.
Apart from my reservations on novelty and impact, I have the following remarks:
1) As the variation from dimer, trimer and tetramer is achieved through a relatively small concentration change of OLAm, the samples clearly have a mixture of all different kinds of colloidal oligomers (Fig. 1, Fig. S3). It is not discussed what the yield distribution of dimers/trimers/tetramers is and how their respective purity changes with the synthesis conditions.
2) In view of 1), how can the authors attribute the optical measurements, both ensemble (Fig. 3) and single (Fig. 4), to a particular colloidal molecule configuration, as in the optical spectroscopy and time-resolved measurements they do not know what the actual crystalline structure of the emitter(s) they measure in these mixtures?
3) What is the quantum yield of the produced materials? This is an important figure that impacts the interpretation of the time-resolved data and in the end all optical applications.
4) Biexcitons:
a. The authors interpret the value of g(2)(t=0) as originating from the molecular nature of the colloids, but this is only true for single excitons. When biexcitons are included in the picture (which they are here in the measurement as no spectral filtering is possible at room temperature), the g(2)(t=0) value actually becomes a measure of the biexciton quantum yield, see https://doi.org/10.1021/nl104054t
b. Why are the biexciton lifetimes so similar for the different species (monomer, dimer, trimer) (Fig. 4m) when long-lived, spatially separated biexcitons with reduced Auger quenching should be possible in the oligomers (Fig. 4o), as observed in CdSe dimers https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-019-13349-1 ? The increase in biexciton quantum yield (see Fig. 4c,g and comment 4) ) would be in line with this.
c. Additional decay measurements should be done as a function of excitation power. Then the particular power-dependencies would potentially allow the extraction of the Auger, trion and biexcitonic contributions in the decay.
5) The first two sentences in the abstract as well as the first three introductory paragraphs and the concluding paragraph in the manuscript are overselling the work and confusing the readers by introducing doubtful connections to biology (“unresolved challenges in understanding the origins of life … prebiotic world”) and molecular chemistry (“expansion of the molecular library within the periodic table … molecular evolutionary chemistry … development of novel molecules”). The authors should not use undefined terms such as “proto-atom chemistry” or the like but stick consistently to the established term “colloidal molecules”.
6) In Fig. 3 i-l, there is a consistent peak at ~410 nm. The authors should discuss where this comes from.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript introduces a simple method to assemble ZnSe/ZnS nanocrystals into a colloidal suspension of predominantly dimers, trimers, or tetramers and reports the properties of these multimers using collective and single-particle spectroscopy. It also demonstrates that Mn-doped ZnSe/ZnS dimers can be used as x-ray scintillators. This work is certainly of interest to the colloidal quantum dot community, and achieving trimers and tetramers of fused nanocrystals without templating is a synthetic achievement. The characterization is thorough, but it does not show strong evidence of wavefunction hybridization between the nanocrystals as the introduction’s analogy to carbon chemistry suggests is the goal of the work. The manuscript also lacks theoretical calculations or discussion of the expected behavior of coupled core-shell nanocrystals with type-I band alignment. With revisions, this work may be suitable for the broad readership of Nature Communications, but it is likely more appropriate for a journal focused on nanoscience.
1. The final paragraph of the introduction makes the claim that the experiments “elucidate the fundamental principles of artificial proto-atoms with specific bonding angles and lengths.” This claim would be better supported by providing statistics on the variation of bond lengths/distances and angles among the species obtained in each type of reaction (dimer, trimer, etc.).
2. Given the heavy emphasis on the analogy with carbon chemistry, it would be helpful for the authors to discuss in one place the data that they believe indicate that their “artificial molecules” exhibit wavefunction hybridization (or as they put it, a “coherent electron delocalization analogy to hybridized atomic orbitals”): 1) The main evidence for hybridization is the redshift of the absorption and photoluminescence. The small size and y scale of Fig 3a-b make it difficult to see the absorption shift clearly. An absorption shift is the more critical evidence for hybridization than a PL shift because energy transfer to the largest nanocrystal in the assembly via exciton hopping or FRET (which don’t require hybridization) can yield the PL shift. Since the oleylamine used to generate the multimers can also lead to Ostwald ripening, would the authors please explain how they can rule out that the nanocrystal clusters are not actually hybridized and are just close enough together to facilitate FRET? 2) There are no theoretical calculations provided to support the idea that the atom-like orbitals of the ZnSe/ZnS nanocrystals are coupled strongly enough to create such hybridization. The authors do compare the redshift of their tetramer to that of the CdSe/CdS dimer in reference 28, but it makes more sense to compare their dimer to the CdSe/CdS dimer to determine if the redshift suggests coupling, as was demonstrated in reference 28 by comparing fused and unfused dimers (which could not be done here because of the synthetic method). Also, they do not specify whether their 71.3 meV value is the redshift of the absorption or the PL. For evaluating hybridization, an absorption redshift is more convincing because a PL redshift can have several other possible sources. Critical to this discussion is the thickness of the ZnS shell that forms a type-I alignment with the ZnSe core and will provide a barrier to wavefunction hybridization. The thickness of the ZnS shell should therefore be reported.
3. The size of Fig 3b also makes it difficult to see the sub-bandgap defect emission around 580 nm. Also, there is a small peak in the tetramer around 380 nm – what is the source of this very blue emission?
4. In the first paragraph of the Results section, “oleic acid” is referred to as a “typical hard base.” The authors likely meant that oleate, the conjugate base of oleic acid, is the hard base.
5. The authors note that “ensemble PL lifetime measurements revealed a dramatic quenching of the lifetime” in Fig. 3d, but these curves appear to be on top of each other. The authors should provide lifetimes from fits to the curves to compare and should revise their description of this data. How do these ensemble lifetimes compare to the lifetimes measured in the single nanostructures? Please also include the excitation power density used for the lifetime measurements.
6. There is a noticeable difference in the sharpness of the image produced using the Mn-doped ZnSe/ZnS monomers and the dimers embedded in PMMA as an x-ray scintillator (Fig. 5i). Can the authors comment on the source of this performance difference since both materials exhibit the same large Stokes shift that avoids reabsorption?
7. It would be helpful to include the relative PL efficiency of the different structures – monomers, dimers, etc. either from single-particle spectroscopy or an ensemble measurement. Ideally this would be PL quantum yield in solution (as is presented in the SI for the Mn-doped ZnSe/ZnS), but relative PL at the same absorption would be acceptable.

This manuscript introduces a simple method to assemble ZnSe/ZnS nanocrystals into a colloidal
suspension of predominantly dimers, trimers, or tetramers and reports the properties of these
multimers using collective and single-particle spectroscopy. It also demonstrates that Mn-
doped ZnSe/ZnS dimers can be used as x-ray scintillators. This work is certainly of interest to
the colloidal quantum dot community, and achieving trimers and tetramers of fused
nanocrystals without templating is a synthetic achievement. The characterization is thorough,
but it does not show strong evidence of wavefunction hybridization between the nanocrystals
as the introduction’s analogy to carbon chemistry suggests is the goal of the work. The
manuscript also lacks theoretical calculations or discussion of the expected behavior of coupled
core-shell nanocrystals with type-I band alignment. With revisions, this work may be suitable
for the broad readership of Nature Communications, but it is likely more appropriate for a
journal focused on nanoscience.
Response: We acknowledge the reviewers' encouraging assessment of our manuscript and its
innovative contributions. We report a universal, template-free strategy for synthesizing
quantum dot monomers, dimers, trimers, and tetramers. In response to the reviewers’ guidance,
we have incorporated theoretical simulations. The combined experimental and theoretical
analysis confirms the quantum-mechanical coupling properties of the assembled colloidal
quantum dot molecules. This methodology can be broadly applied to construct polymeric
libraries of diverse semiconductor core-shell nanocrystals, with details provided in the
following sections.. Therefore, we believe the revised manuscript is well-suited for Nature
Communications.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: I think the authors answered my questions and revised the manuscript sufficiently. In my opinion the manuscript is ready for publication in Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors did an excellent job in addressing all the comments with a lot of new, convincing data and providing a much-improved manuscript. A particular, fundamental concern was the specificity of the synthesis variants for the dimer/trimer/tetramer. Now the new statistics confirms that it is high, proving that the results are not obtained from uncontrolled mixtures, and furthermore, also highlighting the quality and significance of this template-free approach. In conclusion, I now fully support publication in Nature Communications.
The authors might want to consider the following minor formal points for their final version:
- Both in Supplementary Figure 3 and Supplementary Table 2 it should be made clear that the x-axis labels and the column labels, respectively, are referring to the synthesis variant (“target”), whereas the identical labels for the bars / table-rows are referring to the measured fraction.
- In the caption of Supplementary Figure 21 it is stated that “<N> increases from top to bottom for the three decay curves”. However, this is only true for their ordering in the figure legend, not the curves themselves. Therefore, I recommend adapting the legend and the description.
- I like the revised title much better, but it may be good to include the nanocrystal aspect in order to avoid ambiguity, e.g. “Self-organized artificial molecules from colloidal nanocrystals”.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors have addressed my concerns and significantly strengthened their manuscript with theory and key experiments.
In my opinion, there is sufficient novelty in their template-free approach to synthesizing colloidal quantum dot molecules and comprehensive characterization to merit publication in Nature Communications. The abstract and introduction would benefit from further language editing, however.
A few minor revisions:
1. One aspect that Reviewer 2’s emphasis on biexciton lifetimes brought to my attention was the relatively long biexciton lifetimes of ~2 ns measured in even the individual ZnSe/ZnS nanocrystals (localized biexciton lifetime). This was not commented upon by the authors but has been recently explained in the literature by an unintentionally alloyed ZnSe and ZnS shell that reduces Auger recombination and therefore lengthens the biexciton lifetime. I would suggest that the authors include a brief note about this and cite Lin, X. et al. Nature Nanotech. 20, 229-236, 2025 (doi: 10.1038/s41565-024-01812-0).
2. Please define the bond length more exactly in Figure S4 – your nanocrystals are not elongated, so is the measurement center-to-center or center-to-edge, as suggested by the cartoon?
3. The authors demonstrate quite high structural purity of their samples with regard to dimer, trimer, etc., so it remains puzzling that their ensemble lifetimes (Fig. 3d) are so similar when their single-structure lifetimes are not (Fig. 4d-f). The lifetime is likely quite sensitive to the strength of the coupling, so perhaps while the structural purity is there, the uniformity in coupling within the structures is not? Perhaps the authors can comment on the dispersion of single-structure lifetimes they observed to resolve the apparent discrepancy between the ensemble and single-structure measurements.
4. Ostwald is missing from the initial definition of OR in the text
5. Oleylamine in Fig. 1 is misspelled
6. Figure 3f could use an energy scale/labels on the y-axis. Please label the y-axis of Fig 3g - Absorption Red Shift (to distinguish from PL).

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Designing colloidal assemblies with molecule-like architectures comprising more than two electronically coupled quantum dots has often required technologically complex, expensive, and top-down nanofabrication. Here we demonstrate a one-pot chemical synthesis of dimeric, trimeric, and tetrameric assemblies of coupled molecule-like quantum dots (CMQDs), using ZnSe@ZnS quantum dots as model. We show that the “valence” of these “artificial atoms” can be readily tuned by the amount of a suitable ligand in the reaction mixture, and that high-temperature fusion yields highly ordered oriented attachment and strong electron coupling between bound QDs. The shapes of the fused assemblies echo the canonical sp-, sp²-, and sp³-hybridization motifs and can be interpreted as appropriately shaped confining potential wells for electrons and holes. This work establishes an experimentally accessible entry point to related “artificial molecules” with controllable chemical composition, geometry, and electronic structure. The enhanced or emergent properties of such nanomaterials are anticipated to advance applications in optoelectronics, sensing, and quantum photonic technologies.

---

## Introduction

All modern technology is unthinkable without scientists’ ability to arrange atoms into specific molecules/matter with precise control over chemical composition, geometry, and as a result, electronic structure. That same “control mindset” is now being transferred to nanoscale building blocks. For example, semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are widely viewed as artificial atoms1-4 because quantum confinement gives them discrete, atom-like electronic structure, tunable by size, composition, and surface chemistry. Such paradigm has already inspired several applications of QDs as lasers,5single-photon sources,6 source of entangled photon pairs.7 However, fully exploiting the potential of artificial atoms requires learning how to synthesize quantum dot “molecules” with controlled stoichiometry, programmed geometry, and engineered electronic coupling between bound QDs. The latter generates emergent “molecular” electronic states and functions beyond those of isolated artificial atoms,8-13 thus enabling the design of new materials and devices for optoelectronics, quantum photonics, nanoscale energy/charge transport technologies and many other fields.

Molecule-like quantum dot assemblies can be differentiated by the nature of the inter-QD linkage. We define self-assembled quantum dot molecules as finite, stoichiometrically and geometrically distinct QD aggregates whose integrity is governed primarily by the interactions of function al groups on their periphery. To date, several successful strategies have been developed for the programmed synthesis of assembled quantum dot molecules, relying on DNA-encoded recognition motifs,14-16 electrostatic comple mentarity of charged polymer brushes,17 or templated multi-step procedure that allows to bind two QD particles with short covalent links (≈1 nm).18 All such linkages can provide exquisite control over the directionality, connectivity, and symmetry of assembled quantum dot molecules, but they inevitably impede inter-dot electronic communication.19

In contrast, in coupled colloidal molecule-like quantum dots (CMQDs),20 adjacent QD “atoms” form direct core–core junctions, yielding a rigid, chemically robust backbone of fused QDs and enabling direct electronic and energy coupling and, potentially, dopant exchange across the entire CMQDs. Yet, the reliable synthesis of such coupled dots21 remains considerably less straightforward than the assembly of assembled quantum dot molecules. Direct nanofabrication via molecular beam epitaxy,22, 23 though precise and compatible with convenient fabrication of CMQDs-based devices, is technologically complex, expensive, and difficult to scale. Much more practical is a templated approach24 in which assembled quantum dot molecules with short covalent linkages serve as intermediates for subsequent fusion into CMQDs. While reliable, this workflow is experimentally involved and was only extended to dimeric assembled quantum dot assembles.

In this work, we present a template-free, one-pot methodology for the synthesis of CMQDs via controlled fusion of two, three, or four QDs. ZnSe@ZnS quantum dots (Figure 1a) and their Cu- or Mn-doped variants were used to demonstrate our approach and to test the basic properties of the synthesized CMQDs. The exact outcome of the synthesis depends on the optimized amount of added oleylamine (OLAm). Atomic-resolution imaging corroborates face-to-face oriented attachment (OA) of the fused nanoparticles and allows us to postulate a dynamic combinatorial transformation of closely packed dimeric, triangular, and tetrahedral assembled quantum dot intermediates, as the connectivity (“valency”) of each individual QD increases with increasing OAm quantity. The fused CMQDs backbones can be viewed as continuous confining potential wells for electrons and holes, with overall geometries reminiscent of the canonical linear, trigonal, and tetrahedral motifs associated with sp, sp², and sp³ hybridization, respectively. In addition to advanced optical characterization, these quantum dot assemblies were evaluated as X-ray scintillators.

---

## Results

Synthesis of colloidal molecule-like assemblies
The fabrication of CMQDs was derived from colloidal ZnSe/ZnS core/shell QDs25, 26 via modulation of the Ostwald ripening (OR), oriented attachment (OA), and multistep oriented attachment (MOA) process (Figure 1a and Supplementary Fig.1). Briefly, oleate and OLAm, as typical hard bases, exhibit strong coordination with zinc ions (borderline Lewis acids), resulting in effective passivation of the ZnSe/ZnS surface and the formation of monodisperse QDs.27 Meanwhile, OLAm acts as an amine-based anchor, whereas oleic acid (OLA) predominantly appears as a monodentate carboxylate that links the long-chain alkyl tail to the QD surface, with the carboxylate remaining more stable than the amine even in the monodentate form.28 Thus, when the solvent is exchanged from OLA/OLAm to pure OLAm, the passivation effect becomes insufficient, resulting in enhanced oriented attachment and the formation of ZnSe/ZnS dimers.29 When excess pure OLAm is introduced into the system, the viscosity of the reaction medium increases significantly,28 reducing the diffusion rate of the building blocks and promoting a MOA process, accompanied by Ostwald ripening and the formation of timer and tetramer ZnSe/ZnS molecules (Supplementary Figs. 2-5). Therefore, as the OLA concentration decreases and the OLAm amount increases, the self-organized, self-driven structure formed via multistep oriented attachment leads to the predominant formation of tetramer ZnSe/ZnS QDs.

Characterization and binding relationship analysis
We selected colloidal monomer ZnSe/ZnS QDs as the fundamental building blocks. The dimer, trimer, and tetramer colloidal molecules were fabricated in analogy with the sp, sp², and sp³ hybrid atomic orbitals, respectively (Figure 1b). The morphology of the ZnSe/ZnS CMQDs is depicted in Figure 1c-n and Supplementary Fig. 6. The monomer ZnSe/ZnS QDs were synthesized using the hot-injection method, with slight modifications based on refs.30-34 (see Methods). As depicted in Figure 1c-e, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), and high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF-STEM) imaging confirmed the fabrication of monomer QDs with low dispersity in size of 8.4 ± 1.9 nm (Supplementary Fig. 6). Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern and X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) measurements indicate the zinc blende (ZB) structure of the ZnSe/ZnS QD building blocks (Supplementary Fig. 6). The dimer (Figure 1f-h), timer (Figure 1i-k), and tetramer (Figure 1l-n) structures were further characterized. HAADF-STEM images show that the fabricated monomer, dimer, trimer, and tetramer colloidal molecules closely resemble the hybridization atomic orbital model, including similarities in bond angles. Consequently, by decreasing the amount of OLA and increasing the amount of OLAm, the OR process is suppressed, allowing the OA and multistep OA processes to dominate, thereby facilitating the synthesis of ZnSe/ZnS CMQDs.

The fine structure of the ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs was further characterized using HAADF-STEM imaging and the corresponding 3D reconstructed structure. As shown in Figure 2a, the low index atomic planes (111), (020), and (202) are clearly visible, which facilitates identification of the boundary faces of the monomer crystal model (Figure 2b). Fast Fourier transform (FFT) analysis and the FFT-filtered reconstructed atomic structure (Supplementary Fig. 7) confirmed the zinc blende (ZB) ZnSe@ZnS structure along the [101] zone axis (ZA). To further validate the constructed monomer crystal model, structural analysis along the [01̅0] ZA was depicted in Supplementary Fig. 8. This analysis demonstrates the accurate reconstruction of cubic motifs35, which will serve as the model structure for subsequent oriented attachment relationship analysis.

The structure of the coupled colloidal ZnSe@ZnS dimer molecules (Figure 2c) was confirmed through HAADF-STEM imaging, which revealed a continuous atomic lattice formed between the two adjoined monomer QDs. This observation confirms the dimer structure through mutual modulation of the OA processes. A hetero-plane oriented attachment was observed, characterized by the connection of heteronymous faces: (022) ||(211) , matched well with the 3D ZnSe@ZnS dimer QD model (Figure 2d) derived from the STEM analysis. In this hetero-plane attachment scenario, both ZnSe@ZnS monomers in the conjunctive pair were further analyzed using separated FFT pattern analysis, revealing the fusion axes along [011] ZA and [213] ZA , respectively(Supplementary Fig. 9). Additionally, both homonymous (Supplementary Fig. 10) and heteronymous (misorientation) plane attachment relationships are observed in our system.

The sp2-analog trimer structure was characterized using HAADF-STEM (Figure 2e). It is clearly observed that the ternary structure is formed by connecting of a third monomer to a homonymous dimer QD. Both parts A and A of the trimer structure are aligned along the same [1̅21] zone axis, resulting in the formation of a homonymous plane attachment: (202) ||(202) (Figure 2f, and Supplementary Fig. 11). Notably, the size of the third monomer part (A ) in the ternary QDs is significantly smaller than that of the other two parts, attributed to the highly active vestigial monomer based on the incomplete inhibition of the Ostwald ripening effect. This phenomenon is also observed in the quaternary QD structures (Figure 2g, h, and Supplementary Fig. 12). It is evident that parts A toA exhibit similar geometric symmetry with a twisting or twirling effect along the [1̅21] ZA. Additionally, a fourth smaller monomer connects to the trimer structure along the [01̅1] ZA. This connection helps alleviate surface strain when forming trimer or tetramer colloidal ZnSe@ZnS assemblies with constrained attachment.

Significant surface defects are typically observed during the formation of trimer and tetramer CMQDs due to the combined modulation of the OR and OA processes. These defects36, 37 include stacking faults, edge dislocations, twin boundaries, and grain boundaries (details in Supplementary Fig. 13, 14), particularly in the tetramer structure. Additionally, multi-branched multimer QDs are observed during tetramer formation (Supplementary Fig. 15). Furthermore, energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) element mapping confirmed the core-shell architecture of the colloidal ZnSe@ZnS assemblies (Figure 2i-l), which indicating a continuous distribution of zinc in both the core and shell locations, while sulfur and selenium are distinctly located, signifying the shell and core positions, respectively. Thus, by precisely controlling the effects of the ligands via OR, and OA, and tuning them together, we synthesized monomer, dimer, trimer, and tetramer ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs.

Photophysical properties
The optical signatures of the assemblies were further explored as shown in Figure 3a,b. The coupled quantum dot assemblies exhibit significant red shifts in band-edge absorption and photoluminescence (PL) compared to the ZnSe@ZnS monomer. Additionally, according to the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) pattern, the formation of tetramer ZnSe@ZnS assemblies resulted in an almost pure blue emission (Figure 3c). This emission approaches the limits of ZnSe-based QDs, which still presents a challenge, requiring further investigation. Notably, a red shift of 71.3 meV was observed for the type-I ZnSe@ZnS tetramer compared to the monomer QDs. In contrast, our previous quasi-type II CdSe@CdS coupled dimer structure exhibited only a 26 meV red shift.38 Meanwhile, ensemble PL lifetime measurements revealed quenching of the lifetime (Figure 3d). The calculation results show that the electron and hole ground states in the monomer, dimer, trimer, and tetramer are confined to the core (Figure 3e, Supplementary Note 1, and Supplementary Table 1). The first excited state of the electron is confined to both the core and the shell. The red shift of the dimer, trimer, and tetramer relative to the monomer can be attributed to the coupling of the wave functions in the different quantum dots, analogous to the symmetry and antisymmetric of wave functions in conventional molecules (Figure 3f, g). We hypothesize that the formation of larger molecules and increased volume during the OA/OR combined process may lead to coupling with electron dislocation. This could result in observed red shifts in both absorption and PL, accompanied by lifetime quenching, reflecting the coupling among quantum dot assemblies and analogous to chemical bond-type hybridization seen in carbon-based systems.

To further validate our hypothesis, we conducted femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (fs-TAS) measurements, as depicted in Figure 3h-o. A prominent negative peak (ΔA<0) is observed around 430 nm and is attributed to ground-state bleaching (GSB). This reflects the depopulation of photo-generated electrons in the excitons of the ZnSe@ZnS QDs. When irradiated with a 365 nm pump laser, excitons are immediately generated and dissociated into free holes and electrons in the ZnSe@ZnS QDs. High-energy electrons then recombine with holes within 2.0 ps. Notably, ground state bleaching rapidly decays with the formation of colloidal ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs, indicating a fast exciton recombination rate. This rapid recombination may be due to energy transfer or surface defect trapping processes (Supplementary Fig. 16). Furthermore, a shift in GSB to longer wavelengths occurs as the decay time increases from 2.0 ps to 2.0 ns. This shift is likely due to the QDs’ significant volume increase, which results in enhanced electron dislocation and/or spatial separation rates 39-43and facilitates faster charge separation.

Single-particle photoluminescence spectroscopy
We investigate the PL properties of ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs at the single-particle level using single-particle PL spectroscopy. 44 As shown in Figure 4a-c, the single monomer, dimer and trimer CMQDs all exhibit stable PL intensity trajectories. The corresponding PL intensity histograms demonstrate that they all exhibit a significant proportion of bright states. This indicates that these monomers, dimers and trimers were prepared to a high standard. Due to the QDs' surfaces being passivated, the monomer exhibits a standard Auger blinking trajectory, as revealed by the nonlinear fluorescence lifetime-intensity distribution (FLID) 45 map shown in Supplementary Fig. 17. The corresponding PL decay curves which exhibit a multiexponential characteristic due to the influence of multi-excitons, ionized states, and surface non-radiative recombination, are shown in Figure 4d-f. A multi-exponential function fit yielded weighted average lifetimes of 19.7, 17.5, and 15.9 ns for the monomer, dimer and trimer assemblies, respectively. This gradual decrease in lifetime is attributed to an increase in multiple excitons and surface non-radiative recombination in the dimer and trimer assemblies. Single exciton lifetimes were obtained by fitting the PL decay curves extracted from the bright state of the PL intensity trajectories (Supplementary Fig. 18a-c), and the statistical results are summarized in Supplementary Fig 18d. The average single-exciton lifetimes in monomers, dimers and trimers are 25.3, 26.4, and 26.9 ns, respectively. This indicates that forming multimeric structures does not significantly alter the radiative recombination properties of single excitons.

The second-order photon correlation, (g(2)(τ)), curves are shown in Figure 4g-i and reveal the statistics of photons from single ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs. Under low excitation, the biexciton QY was approximately equal to g(2)(0).46 The g(2)(0) statistics for monomers, dimers, and trimers are in Figure 4j-l, with values clustering around 0.37, 0.58, and 0.65, respectively. Specifically, monomers show a narrow distribution due to high purity; dimers are broader, reflecting slightly lower purity, and trimers are also broad, consistent with STREM yields (Supplementary Table 2). Dimers and trimers have higher g(2)(0) than monomers due to segregated biexcitons (SBX), which are long-lived, spatially separated biexcitons with reduced Auger quenching.47 Biexciton PL decay was further analyzed from the first photon in two-photon events.48 Dimer decays fall into two types: (i) rapid decay fitted by a single exponential, from strongly coupled dimers where both excitons reside in one core (localized biexciton, LBX; Figure 4m and left panel of Figure 4o), and (ii) a double-exponential decay with a fast LBX and slow SBX component (Figure 4n). In strongly coupled dimers, SBX converts quickly to LBX; in weakly coupled dimers, SBX and LBX emissions coexist due to slower SBX to LBX conversion.47 Supplementary Fig. 19 shows SBX lifetimes are broadly distributed due to coupling heterogeneity. Supplementary Fig. 20 reports LBX lifetimes of 1.7 ns (monomer), 2.3 ns (dimer), and 2.7 ns (trimer), with longer LBX lifetimes in dimers/trimers arising from enhanced exciton delocalization that suppresses Auger recombination.

Supplementary Fig. 21 shows the power-dependent PL decay for single monomer, dimer, and trimer assemblies.49 As laser power increases, the decay becomes faster, indicating a larger fraction of biexcitons at higher excitation. Power-dependent decay measurements thus quantify both biexciton lifetimes and Auger recombination, by subtracting high- and low-power decays. The extracted biexciton lifetimes are 2.03 ns (monomer), 2.24 ns (dimer), and 2.33 ns (trimer) (Supplementary Fig. 21d-f), consistent with the LBX lifetimes from the first-photon analysis in Supplementary Fig. 20. It should be noted that the biexciton lifetime can reach up to 2 ns, likely due to an alloyed ZnSe/ZnS shell that reduces Auger recombination, in line with recent report50. Additionally, an excess carrier may occupy the second emission center in the dimer, forming a potential trion (Supplementary Fig. 22). Meanwhile, the dimer and trimer assemblies exhibit more blinking in their PL trajectories due to band-edge carrier (BC) blinking, which is induced by surface defects formed during synthesis.51 Auger and BC blinking are caused by non-radiative Auger recombination and non-radiative BC recombination, respectively (Figure 4p). Additionally, due to the weak PL features, it was difficult to investigate the PL properties of individual tetramer assemblies at the single-particle level; only fast PL decay lifetimes could be obtained (Supplementary Fig. 23).

X-ray scintillator application
To further explore the boundaries of ZnSe@ZnS QD-based CMQDs structures, we synthesized doped ZnSe@ZnS QDs. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 24, the effects of different Mn2+ doping concentrations were investigated. An optimal Mn doping concentration of around 8% was found to achieve the highest PL quantum yield (QY) (detailed in Supplementary Fig. 25). Additionally, Cu²⁺-doped ZnSe:Cu@ZnS was fabricated using a similar strategy (Supplementary Figs. 26, 27). The ZnSe:Mn@ZnS was then used as a building block to synthesize colloidal molecule-like structures.

As illustrated in Figure 5a-d and Supplementary Fig. 28, STEM imaging confirms the formation of monomer, dimer, trimer, and tetramer ZnSe:Mn@ZnS QDs. The XRD pattern depicted in Figure 5e indicates that the coupled assemblies maintain the typical ZB structure even after Mn²⁺ doping. Similar red shifts are observed in the absorption and emission spectra of the ZnSe:Mn@ZnS-based system (Figure 5f, g). Due to surface strain, the PL feature of the tetramer structure is diminished. Meanwhile, the coupled assemblies based on ZnSe:Mn@ZnS exhibit rapid quenching of the PL lifetime (Figure 5h). Thus, the synthesis of ZnSe:Mn@ZnS assemblies demonstrates their versatility and potential application in Cd or Pd-based molecular structures.

Inspired by their fast charge separation rate and potential to avoid re-absorption, we investigated their application in X-ray scintillation. ZnSe is known as a scintillator candidate, particularly in ZnSe:Ag@ZnS materials52. Currently, zinc-based structures are primarily used for α particle detection. However, their use in X-ray imaging or detection is limited due to issues such as in stability, susceptibility to deliquescence, and strong reabsorption effects. We propose that our surface-engineered strategy for colloidal assemblies, which facilitates a fast charge separation rate, will provide promising candidates for improved performance and address these challenges.

The X-ray radio-luminescence spectrum shown in Supplementary Fig. 29 exhibits a consistent trend with the UV-induced luminescence spectrum. This indicates that there is a similar efficient energy transfer process under both X-ray and UV excitation. To demonstrate the potential application of ZnSe:Mn@ZnS in X-ray scintillation, we evaluated the X-ray imaging properties of scintillation films using an X-ray imaging system (Supplementary Fig. 30). X-ray imaging of the ZnSe:Mn@ZnS dimer, compared with monomer samples, reveals that the designed structure can distinguish different spring and SUDA markers clearly (Figure 5i), whereas images produced by ZnSe@ZnS appear blurry and dark. Therefore, the ZnSe:Mn@ZnS dimer system inhibits self-absorption due to its large Stokes shift and exhibits X-ray scintillator imaging performance due to its high energy transfer efficiency. Figure 5j proposes a plausible mechanism for the radioluminescence of ZnSe:Mn@ZnS nanocrystals. During the initial conversion phase, X-ray photons primarily interact with the lattice atoms of the ZnSe:Mn@ZnS nanocrystals, generating a significant number of high-energy electrons and holes. Subsequently, secondary electrons and low-kinetic charge carriers are produced. These charge carriers dissipate thermally through interactions with phonons, resulting in the transport of secondary electrons and holes into the conduction and valence bands52, respectively. However, due to the presence of Mn²⁺, the conduction band electrons do not directly recombine with the holes. Instead, they recombine with Mn²⁺, shifting the luminescence center to Mn²⁺. This behavior highlights the potential application of colloidal artificial ZnSe:Mn@ZnS CMQDs.

In summary, we have demonstrated template-free, one-pot, solution-based route to complex CMQDs. The discovery that the “valence” of artificial atoms can be easily modulated by varying the concentration of suitable ligands enables the programmed formation and subsequent fusion of few-dot assemblies into rigid, electronically coupled backbones of the desired CMQDs. The synthesized dimeric, trimeric, and tetrameric ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs can be regarded as confining potential wells shaped analogously to canonical sp, sp², and sp³ hybridization, respectively. In future work, we will elucidate the molecular mechanism by which ligands with low molecular weight (in the present study, oleylamine and oleic acid) modulate the valence of ZnSe@ZnS CMQDs and adapt this methodology to the synthesis of CMQDs from chemically distinct artificial atoms. Overall, our findings provide an experimentally accessible entry point toward solution-based synthesis of complex-shaped CMQDs, opening opportunities for emergent properties and applications in optoelectronics, sensing, and quantum technologies.
